latest_articles.title: Student Identity Gaps, Perceived Instructor Communication, and Help Seeking Intentions
latest_articles.abstract: Student–instructor relationships play a key role in students’ academic success and well-being. Yet students who experience identity gaps in their relationships with instructors may be less willing to seek help from instructors. This study examined whether perceived immediacy and perceptions of instructor credibility mediate the relationship between student–instructor identity gaps and students’ help-seeking intentions. Undergraduate students (N = 269) at a public university in the Northwest completed a survey assessing perceived identity gaps with instructors, perceived immediacy, perceived instructor credibility, and willingness to seek help. Results indicated that perceptions of immediacy mediated the relationship between student–instructor identity gaps and willingness to seek help. Findings suggest that instructor perceptions may help mitigate the negative effects of identity gaps. Implications for instructional communication pedagogy and strategies for creating more supportive and help seeking classroom environments are discussed.

latest_articles.title: How platformisation transforms public service media: A new research agenda
latest_articles.abstract: The expansion of global digital platforms has significant implications for public service media (PSM), which now operate within a platform ecosystem in which a small number of transnational technology companies increasingly shape the conditions under which media are produced, distributed and consumed. In this introduction to a special issue of Convergence on ‘Comparative Approaches to PSM in the Age of Platforms’ we set out how platformisation fundamentally reshapes the institutional conditions under which PSM operate, challenges the public service remit, reconfigures core values and invites a reconsideration of PSM as a democratic institution. Arguing that this represents a profound transformation, we identify five key dimensions that distinguish platformisation from earlier processes of digitalisation: platforms have created a fundamentally different democratic environment; platforms operate at global scale; platforms create asymmetric dependencies; platforms alter the cultural logics of audiovisual production; platformisation challenges PSM’s normative foundations. Building on the Public Service Media in the Age of Platforms (PSM-AP) project, this introduction argues for the importance of comparative research for understanding this transformation and sets out an agenda for the future of PSM studies based around six core themes: values, ecosystem, audiences, portals, content and role. The introduction argues for the urgency in addressing these themes if we are to understand how PSM—as a systemic intervention designed to drive public and societal value—is to be preserved in the age of platforms.
affiliations: School of Media and Communication, University of Leeds, Woodhouse Lane, Leeds, UK
Center for Studies on Media Innovation and Technology (imec-SMIT), Faculty of Economic and Social Sciences & Solvay Business School, Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Belgium
Department of Media and Journalism Studies, University of Aarhus, Aarhus, Denmark
Department of Journalism and Media Studies, Oslo Metropolitan University, Oslo, Norway

latest_articles.journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
latest_articles.title: Associations Between Adult Attachment and Social Anxiety in Romantic Partner Situations: Does Perceived Dyadic Coping Play a Mediational Role?
latest_articles.abstract: Adult attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance are associated with negative individual and relational outcomes. However, it is unknown whether these insecure attachment styles are associated with social anxiety in romantic partner situations, and whether dyadic coping may play a mediating role in these associations. The current study tested these possibilities. A community sample of adults who reported being in a romantic relationship ( N = 88) completed measures of adult attachment, dyadic coping style of their partner, and a newly developed measure of social anxiety for romantic partner situations. Attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance were significantly and positively associated with social anxiety in romantic partner situations. Perceived negative dyadic coping partially mediated these associations, whereas perceived supportive dyadic coping did not mediate these associations. These findings suggest that an individual’s insecure attachment style is associated with higher social anxiety levels in relation to their romantic partner, and this association is in part accounted for by the perception of negative dyadic coping of the partner in response to stressors within the relationship. The findings also highlight the importance of relationship-based mediators in explaining links between insecure adult attachment styles and their outcomes.

latest_articles.title: Constantly Connected, Differently Affected: Response Speed Shapes Parents’ and Adolescents’ Feelings of Connection
latest_articles.abstract: Response speed in digital communication serves as a signal of availability, yet past research has overlooked how speed expectations in specific relationships translate into social connection. This study addresses this oversight by integrating theoretical perspectives on constant connectivity and chronemics to test the implications of perceived response speed for parent-adolescent relationships. Using a 28-day dyadic daily diary design of 142 parent-adolescent dyads, we examined how one’s own and one’s partner’s perceived response speed were associated with feelings of connection. Results revealed asymmetric and interdependent patterns. Faster response speed perceptions predicted greater connection, but these associations were more pronounced for parents. Additionally, parents’ perceptions of adolescents’ response speed predicted adolescents’ feelings of connection. These findings indicate that response speed perceptions can act as a mechanism that links connectivity to social connection in everyday life, but this depends on relational role.
affiliations: The Ohio State University, Columbus, USA

latest_articles.title: Two Paths of Conversation: How Stories and Statistics are Associated With Community Engagement in Online Debate Surrounding Vaccine Science Skeptical Content
latest_articles.abstract: Statistical and narrative evidence represent two distinct ways of substantiating claims in public reasoning, but does this distinction matter for how people engage with vaccine science skeptical (VSS) content and the discursive spaces surrounding it? This study addresses this question through a large-scale, LLM-assisted observational analysis of online engagement with VSS posts and comments that support or counter such content using statistical versus narrative evidence in the Reddit community r/DebateVaccines . Building on Fisher’s distinction between rational and narrative paradigms , we theorize two paths of conversation through which evidentiary forms are associated with audience engagement with contentious vaccine discourses in a naturalistic social media setting: a rational pathway, marked by concentrated participation and corrective contestation around statistical claims and counterclaims, tending toward a single evidence-based truth “approved” by one-click reactions; and a narrative pathway, characterized by generative engagement featuring broader and more distributed participation, more discursive and generative engagement, and greater acceptance of competing viewpoints. These findings provide a springboard for theorizing evidentiary form as a key epistemic logic associated with how conversations evolve in real-world engagement with contentious, socially consequential issues such as vaccine misinformation, while informing hybrid approaches to addressing skepticism toward established vaccine science.
affiliations: Florida State University, Tallahassee, FL, USA

latest_articles.title: Examining the Impact of Perceived Patient-Centered Communication and Institutional Trust on Digital Health Engagement Behaviors
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between perceived patient-centered communication, institutional trust, and digital health engagement behaviors. Specifically, we examine whether patient-centered communication is associated with digital health engagement behaviors: a) viewing test results, b) reading clinical notes, and c) sharing health data with providers, and whether institutional trust is associated with these relationships. Data used were from the 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey cycle 7. Path analysis was conducted using the lavaan package in R. Out of the 3,475 participants, perceived patient-centered communication significantly predicted sharing health data. Patient-centered communication influenced patients' use of online medical records to view test results indirectly through institutional trust, suggesting that trust may play a selective role in certain health engagement behaviors. Results have practical implications for designing communication strategies, underscoring the importance of both interpersonal communication and institutional trust in promoting active digital health engagement. This study contributes to a better understanding of factors related to how patients engage with digital healthcare systems, providing insights into how communication experiences and institutional trust may shape digital health participation.

latest_articles.title: Why Do Young Adults Turn to YouTube for Diet and Exercise Information? A Comprehensive Model of Information Seeking Approach
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines why U.S. young adults (18-29) frequently rely on YouTube for diet and exercise information, drawing on the comprehensive model of information seeking (CMIS) as a guiding framework. Using a national survey of 508 respondents, we found that health consciousness, internet self-efficacy, convenience motivations, perceived credibility, and perceived vividness significantly predict perceived utility of YouTube. In turn, perceived utility mediates the relationship between these key antecedents and health information-seeking behaviors. These findings underscore the importance of platform-specific factors, particularly vividness and convenience in shaping health communication strategies aimed at young adults. From a theoretical standpoint, the results expand CMIS by highlighting how interactive, user-generated media environments can amplify or alter traditional predictors of information-seeking. Practically, they suggest that designing YouTube content to be both visually engaging and trustworthy may enhance user perceptions of utility and ultimately encourage healthier behaviors. Overall, this study sheds light on how young adults navigate digital resources and offers valuable insights for improving online health interventions.

latest_articles.title: Religious information repertoires in Switzerland’s hybrid information environment: asymmetric associations with trust and reputation
latest_articles.abstract: In hybrid media environments, public understanding emerges from patterned combinations of legacy news media, digital platforms, and interpersonal communication. Rather than relying on single channels, individuals assemble repertoires of mediated sources, interpersonal encounters, and direct personal experiences that structure how they make sense of public issues and evaluate social groups. Religion provides an instructive case: as a morally charged and contested domain, it circulates across hybrid media environments while also being shaped by biographical and interpersonal experience. Drawing on a Swiss online survey conducted in 2024 (N = 1,000), we use latent class analysis (LCA) to identify six religious information repertoires based on patterns of digital media use, legacy news consumption, and interpersonal experience. These repertoires are associated with distinct patterns of trust and reputation across Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, and Buddhism. Overall, this study advances research on hybrid media environments by showing that combinations of various sources function as infrastructures of public evaluation. The findings indicate that legacy news media and interpersonal experience remain central, while digital-born sources play a more selective role. The study refines repertoire theory and illustrates how everyday information behavior is associated with social recognition and mistrust, with implications for the social-relational foundations of cohesion in pluralistic societies.

latest_articles.title: Witnessing Gaza: Communicational catalysis and the colonial epistemology of grievability
latest_articles.abstract: Edward Said’s “Permission to Narrate” (1984) showed that Palestinians are systematically denied the authority to tell their own story in Western media. The 2023–2025 events in Gaza—characterized by genocide scholars and the UN Special Rapporteur as meeting Genocide Convention thresholds and subjected to ICJ provisional measures protecting Palestinians’ plausible rights—tested Said’s diagnosis at maximum intensity. Palestinian testimony circulated globally despite massive suppression: nearly 200 journalists and media workers killed, 23 communication blackouts, and more than 127,000 accounts suspended. Yet testimony produced not resolution but a stark split: unprecedented solidarity on one side, intensified complicity on the other. As Judith Butler writes, the “differential allocation of grievability” decides which lives are mourned and which are rendered expendable. Gaza testimony forced this allocation into institutional visibility in ways that existing media witnessing theory has not explained. Drawing on Said’s media epistemology, Mbembe’s necropolitics, and Quijano’s coloniality of power, the article develops three contributions: communicational catalysis (testimony forcing institutional declaration), witnessing as decolonial praxis (seizing the permission to narrate Said showed was denied), and moral latency (the recognition-to-action gap, structured by colonial position rather than information or psychology).
affiliations: California State University, Los Angeles, CA, USA

latest_articles.title: Are Chinese scientists willing to engage with the public on genetically modified foods?
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing on survey data from 321 Chinese scientists, this study investigates their willingness to engage on a controversial topic, namely, genetically modified foods. Extending the Theory of Planned Behavior with topic-specific beliefs, we analyze how six key factors shape engagement intentions: attitudes toward public engagement, perceived institutional and peer climates, perceived self-efficacy, scientists’ own attitude toward genetically modified foods, and their perception of public attitudes toward genetically modified foods. Results of partial least squares structural equation modeling reveal that attitude toward public engagement and perceived self-efficacy are the strongest predictors, while subjective norms play a limited role. Crucially, scientists’ own favorable attitudes toward genetically modified foods exert an indirect, positive effect on their engagement intentions. We further examine disciplinary differences in public engagement beliefs and find that agricultural and biological scientists hold significantly more positive attitudes toward engaging the public on genetically modified foods than scientists in other disciplines.
affiliations: Department of Agricultural Economics, Ghent University, Belgium
Department of Administrative Sciences, Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, Porto Alegre, Brazil
Department of Agricultural Economics, University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, USA

latest_articles.title: Shaping science and society through law: Governance logic and public roles in the revised Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Popularization of Science and Technology
latest_articles.abstract: In this article, the 2002 and 2024 revised editions of the Law of the People’s Republic of China on the Popularization of Science and Technology (“the Law”) are examined to explore how the state shapes the science–society relationship. Relevant explanatory reports on the revision of the Law, policies, and central/local materials about the implementation of the first “National Science Popularization Month” are reviewed. Based on four dimensions (political–normative, organizational–responsibility, capacity–instrument, and oversight–accountability), the new Law is proposed to promote science popularization from “an educational and cultural activity to cultivate individual scientific quality” to “a basic governance project that serves a powerful country in science and technology, Chinese-style modernization, and high-level self-reliance in science and technology.” Three cases of popularization efforts, urban, rural and mobile, reveal that the Law increases the visibility and organizational density of science popularization. However, the materials also reveal that public participation is defined mainly as visiting, experiencing, volunteering, and cooperating with governance, rather than issue identification, decision-making, or cogovernance. Therefore, two concepts, “legalized science popularization” and a “state-mobilized literacy model,” are proposed, and it is asserted that instead of going beyond a simple deficit model or becoming a participation model, the Chinese case presents a hybrid form of science popularization characterized by law centering, multiorganizational coordination and state mobilization support.
affiliations: School of Management, Northeastern University at Qinhuangdao, China
Hebei Provincial Science Popularization Information Technology Innovation Center, Qinhuangdao, China
Library, Northeastern University at Qinhuangdao, China

latest_articles.title: Social Media Platform Repertoires in Everyday Life: Measuring Social Media Use With Passive Metering
latest_articles.abstract: Social media platforms structure the ways in which billions of citizens access information. Nevertheless, to assess social media time use, most research relies on limited data sources, such as self-reported survey measures or behavioral data from single platforms or convenience samples. Using 6 weeks of passive metering of smartphone and computer activity from a quota sample of Italian adults (18–70, n = 1,457), this study provides a behaviorally measured account of platform-specific social media use across the adult population. We quantify time allocation across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Twitter/X and examine how use varies by sociodemographic factors. Results show that Facebook and YouTube dominate everyday social media time, accounting for nearly three-quarters of consumption, while Instagram attracts comparable average time from a narrower user base, and TikTok shows concentrated usage among younger adopters. Twitter/X occupies a marginal niche. Use is overwhelmingly app-based (>90%), a pattern that browser-based measurement cannot capture. Age is the strongest demographic predictor: Gen Z concentrates attention on Instagram and TikTok, while older cohorts favor Facebook; YouTube shows weak demographic patterning. Gender and education are consistent secondary predictors: women devote more time to Facebook, Instagram, and social media overall, and higher education is associated with lower aggregate use and a smaller share on Facebook and TikTok. Employment and income show null effects. Together, these behavioral, cross-platform figures provide a more accurate basis for weighting platforms by their actual audiences than self-reported or single-platform evidence allows.

latest_articles.journal: Annals of the International Communication Association
latest_articles.title: Are persuasion researchers working towards dystopia?
latest_articles.abstract: A thought experiment is proposed to discuss the difference between theories of persuasion that can be used to persuade anyone of anything vs. theories that can only be used to make the truth more persuasive. This letter argues that much persuasion research aims at developing methods of persuading anyone of anything and questions whether this is a goal that social scientific researchers should want to pursue.
affiliations: School of Communication Studies, University of Tennessee Knoxville , Knoxville, TN,

latest_articles.title: Involuntarily mediatized third place: sustaining cultural practices in China’s post-industrial communities
latest_articles.abstract: Drawing on third place and mediatization theories, this study examines how cultural practices are reorganized under infrastructural withdrawal in post-industrial China. Through ethnographic fieldwork with a Qinqiang opera troupe in a former danwei mining settlement, it analyzes how the erosion of physical venues and institutional support transforms collective participation. Findings show that cultural practices are reorganized through fragmented digital arrangements—WeChat coordination, platform visibility, livestream interaction, and temporary hybrid spaces. Rather than voluntary adoption, this constitutes involuntary mediatization, where mediation becomes structurally necessary when offline alternatives vanish. The study conceptualizes this as the involuntarily mediatized third place, extending third place theory by showing how sociability reconstitutes through distributed socio-technical infrastructures under withdrawal. It argues that cultural continuity persists not through institutional reproduction, but through fragile, intergenerationally distributed mediation shaped by platform logics and infrastructural dependency.
affiliations: School of Journalism and Communication, Sichuan International Studies University , Chongqing,

latest_articles.title: Centralized hashtags, embedded discourse: Two structural logics of youth climate activism on social media
latest_articles.abstract: Youth-led climate action increasingly unfolds on digital platforms, where hashtags structurally connect issues, actors, and publics. Using hashtag co-occurrence data (2022–2024) from prominent youth climate activists on X and Portuguese youth climate activists on Instagram, this study applies link community analysis, which captures overlapping multi-membership structures that node-based clustering obscures. Two contrasting structural logics emerge. The international network exhibits a centralized configuration in which core climate hashtags such as #FridaysForFuture and #Peoplenotprofit occupy bridging positions across issue communities, so that visibility and structural centrality closely align. The Portuguese network displays a more horizontal configuration in which climate-related hashtags co-occur with feminism, education, domestic politics, and art-based activism, embedding climate discourse within everyday publics. Digital climate publics take shape as relational structures produced through patterns of hashtag overlap and cross-issue connectivity.
affiliations: CIES-Iscte - Centre for Research and Studies in Sociology of Iscte - University Institute of Lisbon

latest_articles.title: Victim identity and political consequentiality: Framing migrant and citizen deaths in the Greek press
latest_articles.abstract: Why do mass-fatality events with comparable human tolls generate unequal political resonance? This article examines Greek newspaper coverage of two major 2023 tragedies, the Tempi train crash and the Pylos shipwreck, to assess how victim identity shapes evaluative framing, responsibility attribution, and political consequentiality. Drawing on a within-country comparison of three ideologically distinct newspapers, the study analyses how each event was narrated, politicized, and sustained over time. The findings show that, although both tragedies were covered within a broadly negative register, Tempi generated denser evaluative language, more direct attribution of responsibility, and more durable integration into debates over governance and institutional accountability. By contrast, Pylos was more frequently framed through humanitarian, administrative, or border-management narratives and declined more rapidly after the initial news cycle. These differences were patterned rather than categorical and persisted across outlets. The article argues that routine journalistic framing practices help determine not only how tragedy is represented, but whether it becomes politically consequential as a sustained object of public accountability.
affiliations: Department of Social Sciences, The Frances Rich School of Arts, Humanities, and Social Sciences, The American College of Greece, Greece
Management Department, School of Business and Economics, The American College of Greece, Greece

latest_articles.title: Academic freedom: defending a public good
latest_articles.abstract: This essay, an expanded version of a Presidential Address delivered at the 2026 conference of the International Communication Association (ICA), addresses the global erosion of academic freedom and its implications for communication scholarship. Drawing on a survey of 546 ICA members, the article documents substantial restrictions on academic freedom, alongside widespread occupational intimidation. Most survey respondents have personally experienced hostility or intimidation related to their work, most commonly through social media and personal insults. Nearly half of them report altering their academic practice—e.g., by adjusting their teaching content and research topics or speaking out less publicly. While most attacks originate from the public and political actors, the survey shows that a significant amount of intimidation originates from colleagues and other academics. The essay argues that these findings demand a coordinated collective response, including institutional advocacy, solidarity networks, and recognition of academic freedom as an indispensable human right.
affiliations: Department of Media and Communication, LMU Munich , Munich,

latest_articles.title: Subversive memory work: Reworking journalism and its digital archives to contest dominant memory regimes
latest_articles.abstract: Media scholarship has long established journalism as a form of memory work. Yet conventional journalistic practices, particularly elite-centered sourcing and dominant news values, privilege certain actors and experiences while marginalizing others, producing dominant memory regimes. Drawing on a qualitative case study of the People’s Archive of Rural India (PARI), this study examines how dominant memory regimes can be contested from within journalism. It develops subversive memory work as a conceptual framework organized around two domains of mnemonic power, production and access. The framework identifies four interrelated dimensions, namely everyday witnessing, structural witnessing, cultural witnessing, and accessible counter-memory infrastructure. Together, these dimensions capture journalistic and archival practices that bring the lives, experiences, and forms of knowledge of ordinary people and historically marginalized communities into the journalistic record and make them available for future access. The study argues that subversive memory work contests dominant memory regimes by reworking both journalistic production and archiving practices.

latest_articles.title: Where the World Connects: How Intergroup Contact on Social Media Influences Intergroup Outcomes
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how, following the U.S. TikTok ban and the subsequent digital migration of foreign users to the Chinese social media platform RedNote, mediated intergroup contact with American users shaped intergroup outcomes among Chinese users. Guided by intergroup contact theory and communication accommodation theory, we did two 2 (poster identity: American–outgroup vs. Chinese–ingroup) × 3 (post language: English vs. Chinese vs. both) between-subjects online experiments with Chinese RedNote users (N = 833 in total; Nstudy 1 = 364, Nstudy 2 = 469) to explore how intergroup contact through posts featuring cat images (Study 1) and messages seeking connection (Study 2) influenced intergroup outcomes. Results showed that intergroup contact increased Chinese users’ inclusion of Americans in the self, moral regard toward Americans, and intention to interact with Americans. Such effects were mediated by perceived connectedness with Americans. However, these effects did not extend to broader outgroups—people all over the world. Post language did not play an important role in the process of intergroup contact on social media. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

latest_articles.title: Manufacturing controversies: Media, politics and censoring contemporary art in Australia
latest_articles.abstract: Censorship campaigns targeting contemporary art are increasingly visible in liberal democracies, yet their operation is frequently treated as episodic controversy rather than as a structured social and media process. This obscures how such campaigns are assembled, amplified, and translated into institutional pressures, reshaping the arts sector in disquieting ways. From artists Juan Davila to Bill Henson, this study examines how censorship is produced through the interaction of political intervention, media framing, and social media circulation. While contextualizing gallery-museums as discursive spaces within democracies struggling to negotiate conflicting ideas, I argue that censorship operates less through formal prohibition than through iterative escalation, in which reputational, professional, and organizational pressures accumulate regardless of whether artworks are successfully prohibited. These dynamics produce forms of mediated governance that exceed individual controversies, reconfiguring the conditions through which contemporary art is produced, circulated, sustained, and constrained.
affiliations: Queensland University of Technology, Kelvin Grove, Australia

latest_articles.title: Privileged precarity: Working freelance in the TV industry
latest_articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in the television industry’s freelance labour market, little is yet known about how workers interpret and manage the instability, intermittent employment and organisational ambivalence that characterise these skilled contingent careers. This article investigates the lived experience of freelance television work through qualitative interviews with practitioners in the UK and Australia. It maps the recurrent cycle of employment, unemployment and job seeking that defines working life in the sector and analyses the strategies and resources required to navigate it. The analysis critically revisits two widely used but imprecisely applied concepts: precarity and privilege. By tracing their intellectual lineages and examining their empirical manifestations in television work, the article demonstrates how persistent insecurity coexists with structural advantage. Privilege does not negate precarity; rather, it enables freelancers to endure it – at least for a time. The article advances the concept of ‘privileged precarity’ to articulate this distinctive feature of skilled contingent labour in television production, with implications for understanding similar dynamics in other areas of cultural work.

latest_articles.title: The challenge of diversity in public service media: A case study of Spanish regional Broadcast Video on Demand portals
latest_articles.abstract: As European public service media (PSM) corporations adapt to the platformed context, the challenge of preserving diversity, one of their essential elements of public value, has become increasingly complex, especially in the case of regional corporations. In this context, this article focuses on a Spanish case study and examines how the four Spanish regional PSM with Broadcast Video on Demand (BVOD) services – EITB (Basque Country), CCMA (Catalonia), CSAG (Galicia), and RTVA (Andalusia) – integrate diversity in the design and management of these portals (Primeran, 3Cat, AGalega and CanalSur Más). For an empirical and comparative analysis of the strategies, constraints, and tensions that are developing, the study draws on twelve in-depth interviews with the BVOD managers, content directors, and innovation officers of these PSM online services, conducted between 2023 and 2024. The findings show that online portals offer new opportunities to promote diversity as a multidimensional element of public value that goes beyond cultural representation to encompass governance, production, and programming. The study identifies two diversity management strategies – visible and invisible – each reflecting different operational logics that contribute to the renewal of the social contract between PSM and the societies they serve.

latest_articles.title: Communicative Fractures in Chronic Pain: A Conceptual Model for Health Communication
latest_articles.abstract: Chronic pain is inherently subjective and must become communicable before it can be interpreted, socially recognized, and incorporated into clinical reasoning. Existing scholarship has examined pain expression, interpersonal responses, validation and invalidation, patient-clinician communication, family communication, and communicative disenfranchisement, but these phenomena have often been addressed within partly distinct research traditions. This conceptual article develops and delimits the pain communication fracture model (PCFM) through an integrative synthesis of pain science, health communication, illness narratives, interpersonal validation, communicative disenfranchisement, nocebo research, and pain education. The model distinguishes four analytical communicative registers-bodily experience, communicable expression, interpersonal interpretation, and clinical formulation-and three communicative fractures located in the transformations between them: CF1, expressibility; CF2, interpersonal legitimation; and CF3, clinical translation. The fractures are proposed as analytically distinguishable but potentially overlapping and dynamically interrelated processes, rather than as fixed stages, diagnostic categories, or established causal mechanisms. The PCFM links each fracture to preliminary indicators, plausible consequences, and potential mitigation strategies while accounting for patient agency, legitimate doubt, clinical judgment, and structural constraints. Its proposed contribution is integrative, architectural, and operational, rather than a claim to novelty for previously documented phenomena. The model remains unvalidated, and its value will depend on whether future research demonstrates that the three fractures are observable, sufficiently distinguishable, and useful for understanding chronic pain communication.

latest_articles.title: From Pathologization to Participation: Trans Influencers, Gender Joy, and the Socioecological Reimagining of Health Communication
latest_articles.abstract: In the context of increasing anti-trans health misinformation and legislative attacks on gender-affirming care, this study examines how transgender and gender-diverse (trans) social media influencers are reshaping health communication. Drawing on qualitative interviews with ten trans and nonbinary influencers, we explore how participants use their platforms to advocate for health equity, challenge biomedical gatekeeping, and promote gender-affirming narratives. Anchored in the socioecological model of health, our analysis reveals how influencers operate across individual, relational, community, and societal levels-bridging personal storytelling with systemic critique. While existing health communication research often neglects the role of community-based digital actors, this study positions trans influencers as vital agents in countering misinformation, building trust, and redefining what constitutes "health" in marginalized communities. We conclude with recommendations for integrating influencer insights into healthcare practice, policy, and public messaging, emphasizing the need for participatory, relational, and culturally attuned health communication strategies.
affiliations: New York City College of Technology
The University of Texas at Austin

latest_articles.title: Tracing Dialogical Repositioning in Multi-Perspective Expressive Writing: A Longitudinal Qualitative Case Study
latest_articles.abstract: Research on expressive writing has often focused on psychological outcomes, with less attention to how processes of self-reorganization unfold over time. Drawing on dialogical self theory, this study traces dialogical repositioning within a structured multi-perspective writing practice. Using a longitudinal qualitative single-case design, we followed a university student experiencing psychological distress across a six-week writing practice comprising 12 sessions organized around four recurring orientations: emotional disclosure, cognitive reappraisal, gratitude, and future-oriented writing. The data included 12 writing texts, three semi-structured interviews, and 12 brief post-writing reflections. I-positions were traced longitudinally across the writing texts, with interviews and reflections providing complementary accounts of the participant's writing experiences and perceived changes. Results showed a trajectory from an initially distress-dominated, relatively monologic configuration toward a more differentiated dialogical repertoire. Previously dominant positions became increasingly open to reflection and negotiation, while alternative positions and relational voices gained prominence and interacted in more complex ways. Earlier positions did not disappear but were repositioned in relation to emerging reflective, relational, and future-oriented positions. Multi-perspective expressive writing may thus provide opportunities for the articulation, negotiation, and reconfiguration of positions over time. This study conceptualizes expressive writing as a language-mediated dialogical practice and demonstrates the value of longitudinal analysis for tracing processes of narrative self-reorganization.
affiliations: Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences)

latest_articles.title: When Birth Goes Public: Childbirth Vlogs on Bilibili and Gendered Responses
latest_articles.abstract: Inadequate reproductive health-related information remains a key driver of tokophobia. Video-based social media platforms and nonprofessional content creators are crucial in disseminating embodied and narrative reproductive knowledge in China. Yet, less is known about how viewers, especially men, respond to representations of the laboring body. Drawing on gender schema theory, this study employs structural topic modeling to analyze 36,486 public comments on childbirth vlogs from Bilibili, identifying four overarching themes across 16 topics: (1) General Blessings, (2) Community Support, (3) Childbirth Insights, and (4) Praise of Motherhood. An examination of gendered patterns in emergent topics revealed that female viewers were more likely to share blessings and provide community support that challenged cultural silence surrounding childbirth, whereas male viewers more frequently engaged with discussions on risk perception and decision-making. Further qualitative textual analysis indicated that while informational engagement predominated across genders, gendered divergences in risk perception, decision-making frameworks, and modes of engagement revealed a bifurcated interpretive architecture in which embodied knowing and provider-oriented reasoning constituted distinct orientations toward reproductive content. By investigating a domain long governed by cultural silence and medical authority, this study reveals how lay narratives act as counter-hegemonic interventions, destabilizing established gender norms and illuminating the sociocultural structures underpinning childbirth knowledge.

latest_articles.title: Socioeconomic frames of Russia's post-2022 migration to Kazakhstan: A four-language news comparison
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines how Kazakh-, Russian-, Turkish-, and English-language news media framed migration from Russia to Kazakhstan after the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine and Russia's September 2022 mobilization. A qualitative comparative framing analysis of 26 news texts published from September 2022 to February 2026 identifies five linked frames: urban economic pressure; entrepreneurial and labor opportunity; legal-economic incorporation; social stratification; and adaptation, settlement, or return. The analysis situates these representations within Kazakhstan's long border and dense political, economic, and linguistic ties with Russia, while distinguishing border entries from durable settlement. It finds that apparently neutral socioeconomic reporting can both register local resentment and depoliticize it: migrants become conditionally legitimate when represented as skilled, solvent, documented, and incorporable, yet disruptive when associated with housing inflation and unequal access. The study shows how multilingual news publics construct divergent hierarchies of burden, usefulness, and belonging around the same migration episode.

latest_articles.title: Flip-Flopping on DEI: How Can Business Leaders Communicate Ethically About Changing Values?
latest_articles.abstract: Corporate leaders use corporate social responsibility (CSR) communication to build trust with stakeholders. Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs are one type of CSR. In 2021 and 2022, there was a surge in DEI programming at many U.S. companies. However, between 2024 and 2025, some of those same companies reduced their DEI programs, appearing to flip-flop on previously stated corporate values. This qualitative analysis of 43 corporate statements examined strategies and tactics corporate leaders used to address these changes. Five strategies emerged: ignore, withhold, downplay, justify, and repent. Ignore strategies do not acknowledge changes in position. Withhold strategies announce changes without giving any context or explanation. Downplay strategies acknowledge changes while minimizing their significance. Justify strategies argue that change are necessary to uphold important values. Repent strategies repudiate previous positions as a mistake. The ethics of these strategies were evaluated using Baker and Martinson’s (2001) TARES test, which offers five principles for ethical persuasion: truthfulness, authenticity, respect, equity, and social responsibility. In general, flip-flop strategies that foster more open communication with stakeholders were found to be more ethical than strategies that suppress communication. A list of questions was developed to help leaders consider the ethical implications of their strategic communication choices.
affiliations: Texas Christian University, Fort Worth, TX, USA

latest_articles.title: Legal Tactics Versus Communication Strategy: The Ethics of Arbitration Clauses in Crisis Management
latest_articles.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly deploy mandatory arbitration clauses in their terms of use (TOUs) to channel user disputes into private resolution, shielding conflicts from public view while blocking class actions. We argue that TOU-based arbitration raises ethical dilemmas for strategic communication: by privatizing disputes in advance, platforms may prioritize legal risk containment over transparent stakeholder engagement. Drawing on Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT) and the READINESS framework, we show that both frameworks assume an organization retains the capacity to respond when a crisis arrives, and we examine how arbitration constrains that capacity before any crisis emerges. Arbitration strategies create practical and ethical tensions with accommodative responses such as apology and corrective action, and they occupy an ethical “twilight zone” of legally sanctioned opacity. Such strategies may even exacerbate the informational conflicts and reputational costs characteristic of “sticky” crises. Using a trained classifier with an original longitudinal corpus of 861 TOUs from fifty major platforms, we document the proliferation of arbitration clauses in the digital marketplace over time. Our interdisciplinary analysis identifies arbitration as a pre-crisis blind spot in crisis communication theory and a question of ethical leadership for communication professionals navigating tensions between legal containment and stakeholder trust.

latest_articles.title: Moral Courage vs. Moral Deference: Ethical Leadership and Employee Outcomes During AI-Assisted Internal Crises
latest_articles.abstract: This study examines how leadership stance and AI disclosure shape employee responses to CEO communication during an internal, value-based crisis. It further examines the mediating roles of perceived message sincerity and negative moral emotions and the moderating role of employees’ perceived risk. Drawing on ethical leadership theory, workplace courage research, and costly signaling theory, this study employed a 3 (leadership stance: courage-emphasis vs. adaptation-emphasis vs. deference-emphasis) × 2 (AI disclosure: disclosed vs. not disclosed) between-subjects online experiment with 570 participants recruited via CloudResearch. Results showed that courage-emphasis messages generated higher perceptions of ethical leadership, stronger advocacy intentions, and greater perceived organizational READINESS than adaptation- or deference-emphasis messages. Perceived message sincerity significantly mediated these relationships, whereas negative moral emotions did not mediate leadership stance effects. Contrary to expectations, AI disclosure did not produce direct effects but interacted with leadership stance, reducing perceived organizational READINESS for adaptation-emphasis messages. Furthermore, higher perceived risk strengthened the positive effects of courage-emphasis messages on perceptions of ethical leadership and advocacy intentions. The findings contribute to ethical leadership and internal crisis communication research while offering practical guidance for AI-assisted leadership communication during internal, value-based crises.

latest_articles.title: When Moral Outrage Strikes: Managing Stakeholders’ Crisis Responses During an Organizational Scansis
latest_articles.abstract: Ground in the moral outrage, scansis management, and crisis leadership literature, this study examines how scansis type (internal vs. external victims), organizational response strategy (apology vs. atonement vs. strategic silence), and age difference shape stakeholders’ moral outrage in response to a scansis-stricken organization. The researchers conducted a 2 × 3 between-subjects online experiment among U.S. adults (n = 210) to examine the effects of scansis type and organizational adjusting response type on participants’ emotional reaction, retaliation intention, perceived leadership integrity, perceived ethics, organizational reputation, and forgiveness intention, followed by analyses by age group to examine any impact of individual difference in their crisis responses. The results provide implications for advancing the understanding of scansis in terms of its nature and relative effects of different adjusting response strategies, and the impact of generational differences. Implications for strategic communication and ethical crisis leadership research and practice are discussed.

latest_articles.title: Institutional sentinel: Journalistic role performance and the defense of media autonomy under democratic threat
latest_articles.abstract: This article develops the concept of the institutional sentinel to explain how journalists may temporarily reconfigure professional role performance when the institutional conditions of independent reporting become objects of political contestation. Existing debates on journalism under democratic strain often frame departures from conventional objectivity as either activism or part of a moral turn. Such binaries overlook a more specific form of intervention: the public defense of governance arrangements, editorial autonomy, and organizational safeguards that enable impartial reporting. The institutional sentinel is defined as a situationally activated role-performance logic in which journalists collectively shift from monitorial observation to defending these conditions when they are publicly framed as being under procedural threat. The article is conceptual and uses the 2025–2026 conflict surrounding Lithuania’s public broadcaster, LRT, as a revelatory vignette. The vignette clarifies three elements: activation under perceived procedural threat within a context shaped by threat fusion; boundedness, expressed through temporariness, role transparency, object specificity, and reversibility; and a defensive paradox whereby institutional self-defense may protect autonomy while exposing journalism to accusations of bias, self-interest, or partisanship. The article offers a mid-range conceptual tool and develops scope conditions and propositions for comparative research on media autonomy, legitimacy, and professional boundary work.

latest_articles.title: What Makes Child Harm Newsworthy? Event Characteristics, Victim Characteristics, and Media Attention
latest_articles.abstract: Media coverage shapes public understanding of social problems, yet harmful events receive uneven attention even when they involve children. This study examines factors shaping media visibility of child harm in Kazakhstan. Using a corpus of more than 230,000 Telegram news posts (2020–2025), we identify 1,571 incidents involving harm to children and estimate negative binomial regression models to test explanations derived from news values and ideal victim theory. Results show that event characteristics predict media attention more strongly than victim characteristics. Fatal interpersonal violence receives more coverage, while systemic failures receive less. Victim age and gender are not significant predictors.
affiliations: L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University, Astana, Kazakhstan

latest_articles.title: More Than Core and Periphery: How a Mapping Approach Can Add Nuance to Understanding the Journalistic Field
latest_articles.abstract: The influx of new (digital) actors and the resulting changes to the composition of the journalistic field have attracted considerable attention from journalism scholarship in recent years. However, much of the discussion about the new, so-called peripheral actors and the traditional mainstream has tended to, somewhat simplistically, assume a certain homogeneity in each. Recently, scholarship has begun to question this dichotomy, pointing to the vast variety of peripheral actors as well as traditional journalists, and instead argued for a more relational spectrum along which to locate all actors in the field. Yet, we still have an incomplete, and, crucially, under-theorized understanding of the different kinds of constellations in which peripheral journalism may exist vis-à-vis the so-called core of the journalistic field. To address this research gap, we draw on photo elicitation mappings of 101 journalistic and journalism-like actors in Austria and relate them to their position in the journalistic field. The findings show that both the core and the periphery are more nuanced, yet there are commonalities in their relational position-taking, which adds to our understanding of the journalistic field’s changing boundaries.
affiliations: Institute for Research on Far Right Extremism (IRex), University of Tübingen

latest_articles.title: Do Malaysian Newsrooms Jump on the AI Bandwagon? Empirical Evidence From Journalists’ Perspectives
latest_articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly promoted as a transformative force in journalism, yet most research on newsroom AI adoption remains concentrated in Western and other well-resourced media settings. This study examines how AI is interpreted, organized, and used in Malaysian newsrooms, offering insight from an emerging Southeast Asian media context. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 20 journalists across six Malaysian news organizations, the article investigates how national AI governance signals are translated into newsroom norms, how organizational resources and managerial priorities shape uptake, and how AI is incorporated into everyday reporting, editing, and verification. The analysis shows that AI adoption in Malaysian newsrooms is uneven and selective rather than uniform. First, national AI momentum has not yet produced strong newsroom-level governance; instead, the practice remains shaped by limited written rules, selective disclosure, and strong human accountability. Second, organizational capacity is patchy, with uneven access to tools, training, and infrastructural support across organizations and roles. Third, AI is used mainly in bounded, assistive tasks such as transcription, translation, summarization, and headline generation, while verification labor is redistributed rather than reduced. The findings identify a typology of newsroom responses—cautious minimalists, experimental pragmatists, and human-gated adopters—showing that Malaysian newsrooms are not simply “jumping on the AI bandwagon,” but engaging AI pragmatically under uneven governance and resource conditions.

latest_articles.title: The coercion of care: Compulsory connectivity in assistive communication
latest_articles.abstract: Assistive communication expands autonomy, participation and social life. Under particular conditions, the capacity to communicate becomes a duty to remain available. I describe this configuration as compulsory connectivity. It arises when mediated output functions as evidence of presence, nonresponse attracts an adverse default and refusal threatens care, support or recognition. Advanced amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and locked-in syndrome provide the central case because augmentative and alternative communication may enable speech, environmental control, relationships and access to care. Bringing disability media studies into conversation with deep mediatisation and digital disconnection, the essay identifies three mechanisms: the labour of legibility, recursive interpretation in care and divergence between technical and relational states. Together they make output perform presence and render silence legible as loss. The normative alternative is protected ambient presence: social recognition without continuous communicative production. A two-layer protocol gives that principle operational form: communication status distinguishes engagement from recognised withdrawal, while an independently governed safety channel preserves agreed clinical safeguards. Smartphone messaging isolates availability pressures under weaker dependence; brain–computer interfaces provide a prospective test of the boundary between detectable neural activity, communicative intent and consent. Accessibility becomes emancipatory when control extends beyond how a person communicates to whether communication is owed.

latest_articles.title: Stress and self-efficacy under artificial intelligence disruption: A mixed-methods study on the usage of artificial intelligence among Finnish workers
latest_articles.abstract: Rapid workplace integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work practices and challenging employees’ self-efficacy and well-being. This mixed-methods study examines these experiences using national survey data ( N = 2109) and qualitative interviews ( N = 54) with Finnish workers. Frequent AI use, AI-induced identity threat, and organizational AI deployment are associated with higher AI strain, whereas AI self-efficacy relates to frequent use, positive AI attitudes, and subjective well-being. Identity threat moderated several of these associations, highlighting the role of professional identity in AI-related experiences. Analysis drawing on Greimas’ semiotic modalities (must, can, know, and want) explains how these patterns are interpreted and negotiated in practice, revealing tensions between perceived self-efficacy and pressures to integrate AI. AI use was often described as voluntary. However, participants anticipated increasing competence demands and responsibility. The findings emphasize the need for organizational strategies that address identity-related challenges and support employee well-being in AI-driven work transformations.
affiliations: Faculty of Social Sciences, Tampere University, Finland

latest_articles.title: Automated Influence: How Social Bots Reshape Discursive Opportunities in Online Activism
latest_articles.abstract: Social bots are an increasingly prominent presence in online protest discourse. We adapt the discursive opportunity structure (DOS) framework for digital protest, refining its dimensions of visibility, resonance and legitimacy to account for platform-mediated discourse and automated activity. Applying the refined framework through computer-assisted content analysis of bot activity in two major protests – Black Lives Matter (BLM) and Extinction Rebellion (XR) – we move beyond treating bots as a monolithic or uniformly disruptive force, identifying competing pro- and counter-protest strategies distributed differently across the three dimensions. In BLM, pro-protest bot content concentrates on cultural resonance, whereas counter-bot content targets legitimacy; in XR, pro-protest bots are used to build legitimacy and participatory visibility, whereas counter-bots more often work to downplay the movement’s salience. The framework’s granularity discriminates between movement types in ways coarser accounts of ‘political bots’ cannot, showing that understanding contemporary movements requires attending to how automated activity is deployed within their discourse.

latest_articles.title: “Well done, My good and faithful servant”: AI-generated religious imagery, white evangelical U.S. American Christian nationalism, and political martyrdom
latest_articles.abstract: Following the 2025 assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, social media platforms became saturated with AI-generated religious imagery framing him as a Christian martyr. This article examines how generative AI intensifies the production of sacred political meaning within white evangelical U.S. American Christian nationalist discourse. Focusing on Senator Ted Cruz's X post depicting Jesus embracing Kirk alongside the caption “Well done, My good and faithful servant,” this study employs rhetorical-iconographic analysis informed by visual rhetoric, iconography, and political theology. The analysis demonstrates how the post mobilizes familiar Christian visual conventions, scriptural language, and algorithmic circulation to frame Kirk's death as divinely meaningful and spiritually affirmed. The image transforms political grief into a martyr narrative while reproducing racialized constructions of sacred authority rooted in white evangelical visual culture. Rather than generating entirely new religious meanings, AI-generated devotional imagery gains persuasive force by recombining familiar iconographic traditions into emotionally immediate and rapidly circulable forms. The article argues that generative AI extends political actors' capacity to produce and disseminate sacred narratives at unprecedented speed and scale, reshaping how political identity, religious authority, and public grief become intertwined within contemporary digital culture.
affiliations: School of Communication, Illinois State University

latest_articles.title: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence in Personal Health Contexts: Investigating Information Seeking Motivations, Information Processing Behaviors, and Behavioral Responses During and After Interaction with GenAI
latest_articles.abstract: Following the advent of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), seeking health information on GenAI has become a more common and flexible approach. However, laypeople's health information seeking and processing (HISP) motivations and behavior on GenAI platforms remain underexplored, particularly given the current shift from search-based activities to more interactive and conversational processes. This study addressed this gap by exploring laypeople's HISP motivations, behaviors, and behavioral responses during and after interaction with GenAI. Using the risk information seeking and processing model as the theoretical framework, the HISP process was explored from a risk reduction perspective to understand how laypeople interact with GenAI to address their health concerns. Think-aloud protocol and retrospective interviews were employed to capture participants' real-time and reflective HISP interactions. Participants were mainly young individuals in Hong Kong. Through systematic thematic analysis using both inductive and deductive coding, we found that participants' GenAI-based health information seeking was shaped by multifaceted factors, including relevant health experiences, perceived health characteristics, affective responses toward health risks, and personal factors such as relevant channel beliefs. Trust played a critical role in shaping how participants processed the provided information and was associated with indicative heuristic and systematic processing patterns, given the information characteristic (medical vs non-medical) and perceived acceptance risks. Emotion sufficiency, information overload, and information affordance were identified as emerging variables and discussed in the GenAI-mediated HISP context. Finally, participants may choose to follow, reject, or integrate the GenAI-provided health advice into future health consultations, considering information characteristics and implementation difficulty.

latest_articles.title: Mediated hierarchies of suffering? International refugee organizations’ public communication strategies for the Syrian and Central African crises (2015–2018)
latest_articles.abstract: As forcibly displaced people become increasingly marginalized, international refugee organizations create humanitarian communication to shape public opinions. Prior research has mainly examined how forcibly displaced people are represented in humanitarian communication, largely neglecting who and what are portrayed. This study examines who and what are (not) represented in the public communication of three major international refugee organizations regarding the Syrian and Central African crises (2015–2018). Drawing on a quantitative content analysis of 1244 press releases and news stories, we identified both hegemonic and partial counter-hegemonic humanitarian representations. The organizations predominantly covered the Syrian crisis, while forcibly displaced people and refugee organizations were the dominant sources, refining earlier studies. The former are represented in conventionalized, sociodemographically skewed ways. This study advances debates on hierarchies of suffering, demonstrating that humanitarian communication reproduces those not only through representational discourses but also through patterns of selection, (in)visibility and perceived deservingness, across and within crises.

latest_articles.title: Everyday Scrolling: Algorithmic Awareness and Audience Tactics
latest_articles.abstract: In the contemporary digital ecosystem, algorithms play a central role in the selection, ranking, and circulation of news and entertainment. Using Michel de Certeau’s theory of everyday tactics alongside Roger Silverstone’s domestication framework, this article builds on recent scholarship that views algorithmic awareness as differentiated, processual, or scalar. Specifically, we conceptualize algorithmic awareness as a continuum of situated understandings through which users recognize, interpret, and respond to algorithmic curation. Drawing from 56 in-depth interviews conducted in Argentina, we propose that analyzing awareness as a continuum helps explain why users deploy varied repertoires of tactics when engaging with these systems. Findings show that higher levels of awareness do not inherently cultivate user empowerment. Instead, heightened recognition frequently yields deeply ambivalent experiences characterized by cognitive saturation, forced personalization, and strategic platform withdrawal, thereby providing an empirically grounded communication research perspective from the Global South.

latest_articles.title: Riding the Waves of Media Attention: Agenda Building Under Scarcity
latest_articles.abstract: How do non-elite actors sustain public visibility when attention is scarce, volatile, and largely driven by external events? This article examines how the families of Israeli soldiers Hadar Goldin and Oron Shaul sought to maintain media visibility and political salience while their remains were held in Gaza between 2014 and 2025. Drawing on a mixed-methods design that combines a longitudinal analysis of 6,370 news items with in-depth interviews with 10 participants, the study identifies four phases of agenda building: strategic silence, strategic agenda building, agenda displacement, and contextual reconfiguration. The findings show that the families used symbolic action, narrative framing, and strategic media engagement to sustain a baseline level of visibility, while major attention waves were triggered mainly by external political developments. This article reconceptualizes agenda building as a temporal process of navigating and riding waves of media attention, contributing to research on agenda building, media attention, and mediated visibility in prolonged crises.

latest_articles.title: The link between three smartphone school policies and students’ mental health: a growth trajectory approach
latest_articles.abstract: Amid growing concerns about smartphones and students’ mental health, schools worldwide are introducing smartphone policies, often without evidence on their effectiveness. This longitudinal study examines how three naturally implemented policies (full restrictions, partial restrictions allowing use during lunchbreak, partial restrictions allowing use during lunch, and afternoon break) relate to mental health across one school year (up to seven waves). Differences were observed at the first measurement wave (two months after implementation): Students in the full-restriction school reported highest depressive symptoms and anxiety. Differences in life satisfaction were also observed without a clear pattern across policy types. Growth trajectory analyses revealed no significant differences in mental health changes over time. Yet, within schools, both the full-restrictions and the lunchbreak school showed increases in depressive symptoms. Life satisfaction decreased slightly in the lunchbreak school. These findings suggest that smartphone restrictions are not a simple solution to youth mental health challenges.

latest_articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence on journalism: How media trust and attitudes toward journalists shape acceptance, trust, willingness to pay for AI news, and support for replacing journalists
latest_articles.abstract: Although AI is advancing rapidly in many fields, its use in journalism is especially significant, as journalism shapes public opinion and fosters democratic discourse. Artificial intelligence (AI), in particular, has attracted attention for its potential to greatly enhance journalists’ work, but also raises concerns about ethics and job displacement. However, previous research has largely overlooked the public’s perspective on AI, even though understanding these views is crucial for predicting future consumption patterns. This study addresses this gap using data from cross-sectional surveys in Spain ( N = 2337) and Germany ( N = 2213), revealing cautious public attitudes toward AI in journalism. In both countries, acceptance of AI in journalism, trust in its output, willingness to pay for it, and acceptance of AI replacing human journalists are moderate to low. Favorable attitudes toward human journalists positively influence views of AI in journalism, while trust in the media shows a mixed effect. Overall, the findings suggest that public attitudes toward AI in journalism align with broader views on AI, with individual perceptions of AI being a stronger determinant than opinions on media and journalists.

latest_articles.title: Love Without Borders: Explaining Why People Interact with National Out-Groups on Tinder
latest_articles.abstract: Despite our tendency to select romantic partners who are similar to us, a growing body of research seems to suggest that online dating may increase the diversity of couples. However, to this day, there is no clarity around what might drive users to cross social boundaries on these platforms. Building on the Theory of Reasoned Action, we propose a model that integrates individual (e.g. attitudes, perceived norms), relational (e.g. intergroup contact, social identity), and platform-specific antecedents (e.g. use motivation, experience) that could explain national-identity-based intergroup interactions on Tinder. Based on a survey with 668 adult Tinder users living in the Netherlands and the UK, recruited through an online panel, we found that norms and attitudes both positively related to intentions to date national out-groups, which was in turn associated with behavior. Intergroup contact positively relates to intergroup dating norms and, in turn, intergroup dating intentions. The strength of social identity and different motives for using Tinder did not influence intentions. Frequent Tinder usage was linked to greater out-group dating intentions, suggesting online dating could lead to more diverse relationships regarding nationality. Findings highlight the role of intergroup contact and social norms in digital romantic settings.
